Assessed theory: theory-5

docs.title: Dimensions
Phenomenon / Effect — Explicit Peripheral
docs.text:
What is Known: Within the horizon-encoded nearest-neighbor hopping-chain analogue-gravity literature, finite-size simulations already explicitly observe that the outgoing spectrum is approximately exponential over a window and that the lowest-energy part deviates first when the outer region is spatially truncated, with an order-of-magnitude IR cutoff estimate and practical guidance to stop evolution before boundary reflections return. Other related analogue-gravity experiments/simulations show low-frequency suppression or late-time contamination, but often attribute it to dispersion/finite duration or simply note reflections without formulating an energy-ordered breakdown rule. At least one superconducting-chain implementation reports reflections and spectral deviations, but its energy-resolved deviations are not consistent with a universal “lowest-energy-first” breakdown in that dataset (low energies look comparatively more thermal than high energies).

What is Introduced: The statement elevates finite-size caveats into a specific, operational regularity for hopping-chain horizons: deviations from Boltzmann form appear first at low energies and late times, and can be summarized by an effective IR scale E_IR(L,BC) governed by chain length, boundary conditions, and outer-region box size; it further claims mitigation by increasing L or using absorbing/impedance-matched boundaries to push E_IR down and delay reflection-induced contamination, thereby widening the usable energy/time window for extracting thermality and entanglement growth.

What is Novel: The existence of finite-size–induced low-energy deviations and a rough IR cutoff scale is not new at the statement level, because it is already explicitly reported (though not necessarily framed as a general “law”) in a key curved-spacetime-to-hopping-chain simulation paper. What remains more novel is the stronger universality/ordering claim (IR-first and late-time-first as the generic earliest breakdown mode across implementations), the explicit emphasis on boundary-condition dependence as a primary control knob, and the prescription that impedance-matched/absorbing boundaries systematically extend the thermal window; however, the superconducting-chain evidence showing larger high-energy deviations than low-energy deviations weakens the universality of the “IR-first” ordering as stated.

docs.title: Explanatory / Mechanistic — Explicit Peripheral
docs.text:
What is Known: Across related analogue-gravity and lattice-horizon works, finite size and non-absorbing boundaries are known to cause reflections and late-time contamination, and more generally finite observation regions/times can limit access to long-wavelength (low-energy) modes. One closely aligned curved-spacetime-to-hopping mapping paper explicitly connects finite outer-region size, boundary prescriptions, lattice parameters, and evolution time to an infrared cutoff scale and interprets deviations from thermality using that linkage.

What is Introduced: The statement asserts an ordered causal mechanism: in finite horizon-encoded hopping chains, the first deviations from a Boltzmann line occur at low energies and late times because boundary reflections and finite outer-region extent impose an effective IR scale E_IR(L,BC). It further proposes a control law: increasing chain length L or using absorbing/impedance-matched boundaries lowers E_IR and delays reflection-driven contamination, expanding the energy/time windows over which exponential spectra and clean entanglement-growth signals can be extracted.

What is Novel: The main non-novelty evidence is that an explicit finite-size/IR-cutoff explanation with dependence on implementation details is already present in the discrete curved-spacetime mapping work (even if not always treated as the headline contribution). Relative to several other lattice-horizon and analogue-Hawking papers that mention reflections or finite regions only qualitatively, the specific 'IR-first' breakdown framing and the explicit mitigation prescription are typically not stated, but appear largely derivable from standard mode-quantization/reflection-time reasoning rather than constituting a wholly new mechanism.

docs.title: Unification — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed set, several works already treat (i) Hawking-like thermality as a near-horizon, surface-gravity/gradient-controlled effect in analogue gravity, and (ii) explicit mappings from static 1+1D curved-spacetime field dynamics to site-dependent nearest-neighbor hopping chains; individual studies then show approximately exponential outgoing/transmitted spectra in specific finite lattice realizations. However, these papers mostly present platform-specific demonstrations or broad continuum “horizon robustness” arguments, rather than an explicit, portable law about how finite size and reflections systematically degrade the apparent thermality window.

What is Introduced: The statement elevates finite-length/boundary effects into a general, cross-implementation rule: in horizon-encoded hopping chains with open boundaries and finite exterior region, deviations from a Boltzmann line appear first in the IR and at late times due to an effective IR scale EIR(L,BC) set by chain length, boundary conditions, and outer-region cutoff, and the thermality/entanglement-extraction window can be predictably widened by increasing L or using absorbing/impedance-matched boundaries.

What is Novel: Given that the horizon→hopping mapping and near-horizon control of effective temperature are already explicit and central in at least one broad mapping paper, and that specific experiments/simulations already show exponential spectra in finite chains, the proposed “IR-first/late-time breakdown with a tunable EIR(L,BC) and reflection-delay prescription” looks like a synthesized unifying articulation of standard finite-size/reflection physics applied to these mappings. In the provided assessments, this rule is not identified as an explicitly stated, established principle in the cited works; it appears instead to be a natural, largely derivable but previously unstated cross-paper generalization.

docs.title: Generalization / Scope Expansion — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed literature, (i) Hawking/Unruh-like approximate thermality and sensitivity to cutoffs/finite-volume/reflections are established in continuum gravity/field-theory and continuum analogue-gravity discussions, and (ii) discrete simulations/experiments commonly acknowledge that finite discretization/finite chain length and boundaries affect how well a continuum thermal picture is reproduced. However, an explicit, general, statement-level law for horizon-encoded nearest-neighbour hopping chains that specifies an IR-first breakdown governed by a tunable scale E_IR(L,BC) and a bounded time/energy window of apparent thermality is not consistently presented as established knowledge in these papers.

What is Introduced: The statement introduces an operational scope claim tailored to finite, horizon-encoded hopping chains: deviations from P_out(E) ∝ exp(−E/T_eff) arise first at low energies and at late times, with the onset controlled primarily by chain length and boundary conditions via an effective IR scale E_IR(L,BC) and reflection times. It further claims that increasing L or using absorbing/impedance-matched boundaries systematically lowers E_IR and delays reflection contamination, widening the extractable thermal (and entanglement-growth) window in numerics/experiments.

What is Novel: Relative to the continuum-focused papers in the set (firewalls/replica wormholes/QES/scrambling/analogue-fluid reviews), the discrete, device-facing scope extension to finite nearest-neighbour hopping chains plus the explicit IR-cutoff/window language is not present and functions as a genuine scope expansion. Relative to the most directly related discrete curved-spacetime and superconducting-chain works, finite-size/boundary effects are discussed but typically not elevated into a generic, ordering-specific (IR-first, late-time-first) law with an explicit controllable E_IR(L,BC); thus the contribution is best characterized as a synthesis/generalization that is plausibly inferable from standard finite-size/reflection physics but not established as a recognized result across the literature.

docs.title: Constraint / Limitation — Explicit Peripheral
docs.text:
What is Known: In the most directly relevant horizon-encoded hopping/chain literature, finite size, open/reflecting boundaries, and outer-region cutoffs are explicitly recognized to cause late-time reflection contamination and to limit the temporal window and spectral fidelity of an extracted Hawking-like exponential/thermal distribution; practitioners sometimes choose readout times specifically to avoid boundary effects. Several related analogue-gravity and curved-spacetime simulation works also explicitly note low-frequency/long-wavelength fragility and finite-window/finite-size artifacts, though often as caveats rather than as a central, quantified law.

What is Introduced: The statement elevates these known finite-size issues into a specific operational constraint: deviations from Boltzmann behavior should emerge first in the infrared (low energies) and at late times, governed by an effective IR scale E_IR(L,BC) controlled by chain length, boundary conditions, and outer-region box size. It also asserts concrete mitigation prescriptions—making L larger and/or using absorbing/impedance-matched boundaries—to lower E_IR and extend the usable energy/time window for thermality and entanglement-growth extraction.

What is Novel: The generic limitation (finite size and reflections spoil late-time signals) is not novel relative to key hopping-chain Hawking experiments and some simulation-focused papers where these constraints are already explicit. The more specific packaging as an IR-first breakdown with an explicit, tunable scale E_IR(L,BC) and boundary-engineering prescriptions appears only sporadically: at least one curved-spacetime many-body simulation paper already discusses an effective IR scale tied to L/d and recommends increasing L/engineering boundaries (making this formulation largely prefigured), while many other papers lack this quantified, IR-first framing (where it is better viewed as a synthesis/standardization of scattered caveats).

docs.title: Conceptual Reframing / Abstraction — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: In the most directly relevant lattice analogue-gravity line (superconducting/XY or fermionic hopping chains implementing 1+1D curved-spacetime Dirac/field dynamics), the metric-function-to-site-dependent-nearest-neighbor-hopping encoding and the interpretation of Hawking-like thermality via a horizon and a local gradient/surface-gravity analogue are already explicit and treated as core conceptual machinery. This establishes that the broader “horizon-encoded hopping” lens itself is not novel with respect to that subliterature.

What is Introduced: The statement adds an operational finite-size organizing rule: in finite open chains, breakdown of apparent Boltzmann spectra is expected to onset first in the IR (low energies) and at late times due to an effective IR scale E_IR(L,BC) controlled by chain length, boundary conditions, and outer-region cutoff, with mitigation via increasing L or using absorbing/impedance-matched boundaries to suppress reflections. It also ties this IR-first deviation pattern to practical extraction windows for exponential spectra and inside/outside entanglement growth in experiments/numerics.

What is Novel: Across the aggregated assessments, the closest prior lattice papers already supply the metric↔hopping/horizon framework (so that part is established), but they do not appear to have elevated a named, general “IR-first breakdown via finite-size reflections/cutoffs” rule with an explicit E_IR(L,BC) control-parameter summary as a standalone organizing principle. The most supported novelty is therefore a higher-level articulation/packaging of finite-size deviation phenomenology that is plausible to derive from existing finite-chain physics and the established mapping, rather than a clearly documented, previously established claim in the core lattice papers.

docs.title: Empirical Synthesis / Meta-Regularity — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed corpus, individual studies report approximately exponential/thermal-like outgoing populations over a finite window and sometimes observe finite-size or mode-structure limitations within a single platform (e.g., discrete Dirac-lattice numerics; trapped/BEC experiments). A review-level synthesis in analogue fluids discusses robustness of Hawking-like thermality and attributes deviations to dispersion/greybody/nonlinear/dissipative effects, but it does not articulate a discrete hopping-chain-specific law that the first systematic breakdown is IR-first and reflection/outer-box controlled.

What is Introduced: The statement introduces an across-implementation meta-regularity for finite horizon-encoded hopping chains: departures from Boltzmann behavior should emerge first at low energies and late times due to a finite-size IR scale EIR(L,BC) set by outer-region length and boundary reflectivity. It further claims a controllability/mitigation rule (increase L or use absorbing/impedance-matched boundaries) that predictably lowers EIR and delays reflection contamination, widening the energy/time window over which apparent thermality and entanglement-growth diagnostics are reliable.

What is Novel: Relative to the assessed papers, the novel element is elevating scattered single-platform observations into an explicit, portable cross-study scaling/diagnostic claim: an IR-first deviation pattern parameterizable by EIR(L,BC) and systematically improvable by boundary engineering. The least-novel evidence comes from papers that already contain pieces of the story (finite-size/mode limitations and exponential windows within one system), making the overall claim plausibly synthesizable from prior results even though no assessed paper is identified as explicitly stating this specific EIR(L,BC) reflection/IR-first law as established knowledge.

Assessed theory: theory-4

docs.title: Dimensions
Phenomenon / Effect — Explicit Established
docs.text:
What is Known: Across holography/SYK/JT and quantum-simulation reviews and demonstrations, “Track B”-style goals are already operationalized by many-body information diagnostics (OTOCs/scrambling, teleportation fidelity or mutual information signatures, Page-curve/Page-time transitions, reconstruction/decoding maps) and by resource requirements such as TFD/EPR-like entanglement and two-sided couplings/decoders. Multiple sources also make clear that these diagnostics can be implemented and measured on non-gravitational platforms, i.e., without engineering an explicit horizon-like effective metric. In addition, there is explicit evidence that some headline Track-B-style signatures (e.g., traversable-wormhole teleportation signals) can occur as false positives in non-chaotic/integrable models, motivating explicit scrambling/chaos validation rather than “horizon-like” reasoning.

What is Introduced: The statement consolidates as a single empirical/operational claim that Track B simulation “success” is defined by many-body information observables plus special entangled-state preparation and decoding/two-sided operations, and that none of this requires any explicit horizon/metric engineering. It also implicitly elevates a methodological stance: do not treat horizon analogues as relevant validation criteria for Track B targets.

What is Novel: Relative to the surveyed literature, the core content (Track B defined by information observables/resources rather than horizons) is already explicit and established in reviews and primary holography/SYK-teleportation work; novelty is therefore low. The most distinctive strengthening supported by the provided evidence is the “false-positive” pressure: commuting/integrable SYK can show teleportation-like signals despite slow/non-chaotic dynamics, sharpening the need for independent scrambling/chaos validation beyond any single signature. That sharpening is better viewed as an added constraint/interpretation emphasis rather than a new phenomenon.

docs.title: Explanatory / Mechanistic — Explicit Established
docs.text:
What is Known: Across core holography/black-hole-information and quantum-simulation literature, Track-B ingredients are already explicitly treated as the operative mechanisms/diagnostics: TFD/two-sided entanglement, scrambling/OTOCs, decoding/reconstruction maps (e.g., Petz/modular flow), and Page/QES-type transitions; several sources also explicitly connect these to traversable-wormhole teleportation protocols rather than to analogue horizon engineering. Some quantum-simulation/chaos papers discuss OTOC measurement and time-reversal operations, but may not elevate the full Track-B “resource checklist” to a central principle.

What is Introduced: The statement packages these ingredients into an explicit operational success criterion for “holographic/information-theoretic” simulations: validate via many-body information observables and require special entangled resources plus two-sided couplings/decoding/time-reversal operations, while asserting that no explicit horizon-like metric engineering is needed for these tasks.

What is Novel: Relative to review/theory papers that already articulate the TFD–wormhole, scrambling–OTOC, and reconstruction/decoding mechanisms, the statement is largely a restatement (low novelty). The most novel element is the explicit, lab-facing contrast claim (“not horizons”) and the elevation of a necessity-style operational checklist, which is only implicit or peripheral in some simulator-focused papers; however, this contrast is still broadly derivable from the juxtaposition of analogue-horizon (Track A) versus holographic-information (Track B) literatures rather than being a new mechanism.

docs.title: Unification — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed corpus, Track-B-style black-hole/holography simulations are already explicitly framed in terms of many-body information diagnostics and resources—e.g., scrambling/OTOCs and chaos bounds, teleportation fidelity/channel capacity, Page-curve/island/QES logic, and decoding/reconstruction maps often tied to TFD/EPR-type entanglement—without requiring any analogue metric horizon engineering. At the same time, most papers do not explicitly elevate a single cross-program operational rule that ‘Track B success is defined by information observables and entanglement resources rather than horizons’ as a named organizing taxonomy separating it from analogue-horizon work.

What is Introduced: The statement explicitly unifies diverse holographic-information demonstrations under an operational checklist (OTOCs/teleportation mutual information/Page-like transitions/reconstruction maps plus special entangled resources and decoding/two-sided couplings) and makes the horizon-independence of these tasks part of the success criterion. In context of the broader dual-track theory, it also functions as one half of a partitioning principle intended to prevent importing Track-A (horizon/spectrum) validation into Track-B (information/reconstruction) claims.

What is Novel: The Track-B ingredients themselves (scrambling diagnostics, TFD/ER=EPR motivation, decoding/teleportation observables) are largely explicit and established in review and core theory papers; thus that content is not strongly novel. The more novel contribution is the explicit, prescriptive operational separation—stating at the principle level that Track-B validation is fundamentally horizon-independent and should be judged by many-body information observables/resources—which appears in the assessed set mostly as a synthesis that can be inferred from surveys/juxtapositions rather than as an explicitly stated, widely recognized taxonomy; ambiguity results (e.g., pseudo-/commuting-SYK producing “teleportation-like” signals) support the need for track-specific validation but do not by themselves supply this overarching rule.

docs.title: Generalization / Scope Expansion — Explicit Established
docs.text:
What is Known: Multiple Track-B (holographic/information-theoretic) papers and reviews already explicitly treat “black-hole-like” simulation targets as many-body boundary dynamics (e.g., SYK/JT-inspired models, random circuits) to be validated by information observables (OTOCs/scrambling, teleportation fidelity, Page-curve/island/QES-style transitions), rather than by engineering an analogue metric or horizon. Several sources also explicitly discuss the practical resource requirements for these diagnostics (special entangled states like TFD/EPR resources, two-sided couplings, decoding/time-reversal-style operations) and show that similar signatures can occur even in atypical model classes (e.g., integrable/commuting SYK variants).

What is Introduced: The statement consolidates this into an operational scope principle: for Track-B simulations, success criteria are defined by many-body information observables and the associated preparation/operation requirements, and these demonstrations can be realized without any explicit horizon-like metric engineering. It further sharpens the “not horizons” separation as a validation rule (i.e., horizons are not the right success criterion for Track B).

What is Novel: As a scope/generalization claim, the core content is largely not novel because it is already explicit and central in key Track-B simulation proposals and surveys (digital minimal AdS/CFT; scrambling-to-simulators reviews), and is also consistent with the broader holography literature that treats information diagnostics in non-geometric boundary models (e.g., SYK evidence alongside JT/gravity toy models). The incremental novelty is mainly emphasis/packaging: elevating an operationally crisp separation criterion (“validate by information observables, not horizons”) and bundling concrete implementation-resource requirements and known confounders (e.g., teleportation-like signals in commuting/integrable or small-N/sparse instances) into a single statement; this latter consolidation is present but more peripheral/uneven across individual papers.

docs.title: Constraint / Limitation — Explicit Established
docs.text:
What is Known: Across core holography/information-paradox works, it is explicitly established that kinematic/thermal (fixed-background) signatures are insufficient to certify unitarity or interior reconstruction, and that entanglement structure and code-subspace/replica-wormhole conditions constrain what “interior access” can mean. Separately, scrambling/OTOC-style diagnostics are widely treated as at best necessary-not-sufficient for holography, and specific counterexamples (e.g., commuting/non-chaotic SYK variants) show that some “gravity-like” signals can be false positives.

What is Introduced: The statement crystallizes these points into an operational validation constraint for Track-B-style (holographic/information-theoretic) simulations: success should be defined by many-body information observables and protocol resources (e.g., TFD/EPR-like entanglement, two-sided couplings/decoding, and chaos/scrambling diagnostics) and should not depend on, or be inferred from, explicit horizon/metric engineering. It also makes the methodological warning explicit: do not cross-apply Track-A horizon/thermal evidence as Track-B evidence (and conversely do not infer horizons from teleportation-like Track-B signals).

What is Novel: As a constraint on what counts as evidence for holographic/information-theoretic claims, the core content is largely not novel relative to the established holography/interior-reconstruction literature that already denies “thermality implies interior reconstruction” and emphasizes entanglement/replica/coding structure. The remaining novelty is mostly in packaging: making a concise, cross-platform, experiment-facing rule about diagnostic separation and false-positive risks (especially emphasizing small-N/commuting/sparse mimics) that many simulation/analogue papers only imply via scattered caveats rather than state as an explicit principle.

docs.title: Conceptual Reframing / Abstraction — Explicit Established
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed literature on holography/SYK/wormhole-teleportation and black-hole information, Track-B-style claims are already framed as being validated by many-body information diagnostics (e.g., OTOCs/chaos, teleportation-channel measures, Page/QES transitions, reconstruction/decoding maps) and by resource requirements such as special entangled states (often TFD/EPR) plus couplings/decoders. Multiple papers explicitly treat these information-theoretic tasks as not requiring any engineered analogue metric/horizon, in contrast to analogue-gravity/kinematic-horizon programs that validate via local spectra/correlations.

What is Introduced: The statement packages this already-common practice into an explicit, prescriptive rule for interpreting and designing ‘holographic-information’ simulations: success is defined by demonstrating scrambling/decoding/teleportation/Page-type observables and the requisite entanglement/coupling operations, and the presence of a horizon-like engineered metric is neither required nor an appropriate validation proxy. It also sharpens the interpretational boundary by implying that importing horizon-style validation criteria into Track B (or vice versa) risks category errors/false positives.

What is Novel: The core content (“Track B is about information observables and entanglement/scrambling resources, not horizon engineering”) is largely already explicit in several holography/quantum-information papers and is at least implicit as standard validation practice in others, so it is not a new scientific concept per se. The incremental novelty lies mainly in elevating this into a clean, track-specific operational criterion and making the ‘not horizons’ exclusion explicit as part of a broader taxonomy; some papers only gesture at this separation peripherally (e.g., warning that certain signals are not uniquely geometric).

docs.title: Empirical Synthesis / Meta-Regularity — Explicit Established
docs.text:

These same sources also emphasize that kinematic/horizon-like or thermal/near-horizon QFT signatures are not sufficient evidence for interior reconstruction or Hayden–Preskill-type information recovery, which instead track entanglement-wedge/QES/replica-wormhole structure and scrambling dynamics.

What is Introduced: The statement packages this established operational viewpoint into an explicit cross-implementation validation rule for Track B: judge success by many-body information observables and required entanglement/decoding resources, and treat horizon/metric engineering as unnecessary for realizing these information-theoretic tasks. It also implicitly functions as a checklist-style prescription for experimental interpretation (what to measure/prepare) rather than a new empirical finding.

What is Novel: Given the strongest counterevidence, the core meta-regularity claimed by the statement (Track-B success hinges on many-body entanglement/scrambling/decoding validators and can be realized without explicit horizons) is already explicitly stated and treated as established in key synthesis sources. It also implicitly draws a boundary on what Track A observations warrant (they are not evidence of decoding/interior-reconstruction capability), though that "false positive" warning is more explicit in the broader dual-track description than in this single statement.

What is Novel: The strongest counterevidence is that essentially this same Track A feasibility framing (metric engineering + local measurements as the dominant requirements) is already explicitly established in core analogue-gravity and QFT-in-curved-space simulation references, making the statement largely non-novel within its stated domain. What is Novel: The kinematics-not-dynamics limitation and the dominance of analog control/measurement systematics for Track-A signatures are not novel (they are repeatedly explicit and treated as established in analogue-gravity experiment/simulation papers). The more novel element is the explicitly stated, actionable separation in terms of required experimental primitives/resources ("no TFD/two-copy/U* needed for Track A" and "don’t validate Track B with Track-A signatures"), which is often only implicit/derivable from the combination of analogue-gravity caveats and holographic/decoding resource analyses—though some holography-adjacent papers already effectively demonstrate closely related “thermality/signature insufficiency” warnings.

docs.title: Dimensions
Phenomenon / Effect — Explicit Established
docs.text:
What is Known: In the most directly relevant sources in this set, the central empirical ingredients are already described: the distinction between “peak-size” vs “size-winding” teleportation mechanisms in SYK-like protocols, the approximately linear-in-size phase of a complex size-resolved quantity q(l) with strong intra-size coherence, and the idea that an appropriate two-sided coupling can effectively “unwind” those phases. Additionally, at least one finite-N/hardware-oriented SYK study explicitly measures q(l) and R(l) and links μ-sign–dependent slope reversal of arg q(l) to sign-asymmetric mutual-information/teleportation performance.

What is Introduced: The statement consolidates these ingredients into a single sufficient operational discriminator/certification criterion with three explicit conditions: (1) linear arg q(l) over dominant P(l) support, (2) R(l)≈1 over that support, and (3) strong μ-sign asymmetry with enhancement when μ cancels the winding. It also adds a prescriptive interpretive rule: teleportation-like signals lacking (1)–(2) should not be attributed to the size-winding (holographic) mechanism, but instead to alternative mechanisms such as peaked-size/thermalization-driven interference.

What is Novel: Relative to the most relevant literature here, the underlying effect claims (existence of coherent size-winding, its relation to unwinding by coupling choice, and associated sign-asymmetries) are not novel: they are already explicitly discussed in the review-level treatment and operationalized/observed in the sparse-SYK teleportation simulation/experiment paper. Any remaining novelty is mainly in packaging/elevating a bundle of already-described diagnostics into a formalized, standalone “sufficient discriminator” and an explicit admonition about attribution, which reads as synthesis rather than discovery of a new phenomenon.

docs.title: Explanatory / Mechanistic — Explicit Peripheral
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed SYK/teleportation-focused literature, the core “teleportation-by-size-winding” mechanism is already articulated: a two-sided coupling can imprint size-dependent phases, and in holographic/SYK-like regimes the phase of a size-resolved quantity is approximately linear in size and can be cancelled/enhanced by the appropriate sign of the coupling, yielding strong sign-asymmetry in teleportation metrics. It is also known that teleportation-like signatures can arise from non-holographic mechanisms (e.g., narrowly peaked size distributions, integrable/oscillatory or thermalization-driven interference), so teleportation success alone is not a unique holographic indicator.

What is Introduced: The statement packages these ingredients into an explicit operational “mechanism certification” rule with three jointly checked conditions: (1) approximate linearity of arg q(l) in size l over the dominant support of P(l), (2) an explicit intra-size coherence requirement R(l)=|q(l)|/P(l)≈1 over that support, and (3) a causal/diagnostic link between flipping the sign of μ, reversal/cancellation of the winding slope, and a correspondingly strong sign-asymmetry in teleportation figures of merit. It additionally makes a normative attribution claim: if (1)–(2) fail, observed teleportation should not be attributed to the size-winding (holographic) mechanism.

What is Novel: The underlying mechanistic picture (linear size-dependent phases, cancellation by coupling sign, and alternative peak-size/thermalization mechanisms) appears explicitly and centrally in at least one broad review, and is analyzed in detail (including competing mechanisms and μ-sign behavior) in commuting/nonchaotic variants, reducing novelty of the basic mechanism. What remains novel is mainly the formalization into a sufficient operational discriminator with an explicit coherence-ratio test R(l)≈1 and a stronger “certification/attribution” reading (a practical decision rule rather than a descriptive mechanism), which is not stated as an established theorem across the assessed works.

docs.title: Unification — Explicit Established
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed corpus, key building blocks are already present: (i) operator-size diagnostics (including size-resolved complex quantities like q(l) and coherence measures like R(l)) in SYK-like teleportation simulations, and (ii) the explicit idea that teleportation-like signatures can arise from multiple distinct mechanisms (holographic/size-winding versus non-holographic mimics such as peaked-size interference or thermalization), requiring discrimination. In particular, a major scrambling/teleportation review and the Commuting-SYK work already treat this mechanism-level taxonomy and contrast as an explicit, central organizing theme rather than an unarticulated synthesis.

What is Introduced: The theory statement packages these ingredients into a single operational certification criterion: require (1) approximately linear phase arg q(l) across dominant support of P(l), (2) near-unity coherence ratio R(l) over that support, and (3) a strong sign-asymmetric response under μ→−μ in the two-sided coupling e^{iμV}, with enhancement when the coupling cancels the winding. It further elevates the negative claim into the same rule: teleportation signals without (1)–(2) should not be attributed to the size-winding (holographic) mechanism and are instead more consistent with alternative mechanisms.

What is Novel: Relative to many broad reviews/white papers and adjacent black-hole/QI syntheses that discuss wormholes, scrambling, teleportation, or experimental platforms without proposing a single microscopic discriminator, this explicit ‘one-rule’ operator-size-based diagnostic is a new cross-cutting unification. However, the least-novel evidence is decisive for the core claim of unification: the review and Commuting-SYK paper already contain essentially the same conceptual unification (holographic size-winding vs non-holographic mimics) and the need to distinguish them, so the novelty here is primarily in explicit operationalization/packaging rather than in introducing a new unifying principle in the most directly relevant subliterature.

docs.title: Generalization / Scope Expansion — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Within the core two-sided SYK traversable-wormhole-teleportation literature, operator-size notions (Pauli/Majorana strings) and the use of two-sided couplings are already in-scope, and small-N implementations are explicitly explored. Reviews and in-model analyses also already emphasize that small-N, commuting, or learned/structured Hamiltonians can produce “teleportation-like” signatures without uniquely certifying a holographic mechanism.

What is Introduced: The statement packages these ingredients into a portable operational certification criterion with explicit applicability conditions: (i) a meaningful operator-size decomposition, (ii) size-resolved phase coherence quantified by linear arg q(l) and R(l)≈1 over dominant support, and (iii) a μ-sign reversal test tied to cancellation of size-dependent phase winding, intended to be used across SYK-like models including small-N digital implementations. It also explicitly delimits where it should not be applied (e.g., analogue-gravity Hawking/Unruh experiments lacking two-sided entangled copies and size-based couplings) and foregrounds practical measurement caveats/proxies.

What is Novel: Across most of the provided corpus (general scrambling/OTOC measurement papers, SYK platform proposals, black-hole information papers, and holography/channel-capacity discussions), this explicit cross-setting certification scope and its “do-not-attribute-without-(1)-(2)” rule is not stated and thus represents a genuine scope expansion relative to those works. However, in the closest adjacent sources (a scrambling review and a commuting-SYK analysis), the logic that size structure and small-N/commuting mimicry limit holographic interpretation is already present, making the criterion’s broad scope and boundary-setting largely an explicit elevation/packaging of derivable implications rather than entirely new content in that near literature.

docs.title: Constraint / Limitation — Explicit Established
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the provided literature, it is already explicitly emphasized (especially in the scrambling/teleportation review and the Commuting-SYK analysis) that teleportation-like signatures (mutual information/fidelity improvements) are not, by themselves, a reliable certificate of holographic/wormhole dynamics: small-N effects, nonchaotic/commuting/learned Hamiltonians, peaked-size distributions, and generic thermalization can mimic similar signals. The Commuting-SYK paper further explicitly discusses regimes where size-winding is present or washed out and notes the exponential/tomographic difficulty of directly accessing fine-grained size-resolved quantities such as q(l) and coherence measures.

What is Introduced: The statement packages these interpretational caveats into a more prescriptive operational certification rule: attribute teleportation to the holographic size-winding mechanism only if (1) arg q(l) is approximately linear in size over the dominant support of P(l), (2) the coherence ratio R(l)=|q(l)|/P(l) is near 1 over that support, and (3) flipping the sign of μ in G(μ)=e^{iμV} reverses/cancels the winding and yields a strong sign-asymmetry in teleportation metrics, with enhancement for the canceling sign. It also asserts a negative diagnostic: teleportation observed without (1)–(2) should not be attributed to size-winding and is more consistent with alternative mechanisms.

What is Novel: When aggregating across the paper set, the core limitation claim (“teleportation signals alone do not certify holographic wormhole dynamics; mimics exist”) is not novel because it is explicitly established and treated as central in both the general review and the Commuting-SYK work. The added novelty is mainly in elevating specific size-resolved phase-coherence conditions (linearity of arg q(l), high R(l)) plus the μ-sign reversal test into an explicit sufficient discriminator/decision criterion; however, the existence and experimental relevance of these kinds of size-winding/coherence caveats and mechanism competition are already explicitly discussed in the Commuting-SYK analysis, so overall this dimension is best judged as established rather than new within this corpus.

docs.title: Conceptual Reframing / Abstraction — Explicit Peripheral
docs.text:
What is Known: Within the closest SYK-teleportation/operator-growth literature in the provided set, the operator-size framing and the distinction between “size-winding” versus “peaked-size/thermalization” mechanisms is already explicitly articulated, and concrete size-resolved complex diagnostics and ratios (q(l), R(l), Qn/Pn, rn) are already defined and used interpretively. In particular, a sparse/chaotic SYK teleportation simulation paper explicitly formalizes q(l) and R(l) and applies them as mechanism probes, and a “commuting SYK” paper similarly operationalizes phase structure/ratios as diagnostics for pseudo-holographic teleportation signatures; a broad review also already adopts the operator-size/winding-vs-peak-size organizing lens.

What is Introduced: The statement packages these ingredients into an explicit operational “certification criterion” framed as a sufficient discriminator: (1) approximately linear arg q(l) over the dominant support of P(l), (2) near-unity intra-size phase coherence R(l)=|q(l)|/P(l) on that support, and (3) a correlated strong μ-sign asymmetry where flipping sign reverses/cancels the winding slope and correspondingly enhances/suppresses teleportation figures of merit. It also elevates the interpretive rule “teleportation without (1)–(2) should not be attributed to size-winding” as the key abstraction, i.e., a mechanism-classification lens rather than treating teleportation peaks alone as evidence.

What is Novel: Aggregating across papers, the dominant limiting evidence comes from the most relevant SYK-teleportation papers: they already contain essentially the same operator-size phase/coherence objects (q(l)/R(l) or close analogues) and use them diagnostically, which makes the present contribution largely a consolidation/standardization into a single triad-style operational test rather than a new abstraction. Relative to many broader black-hole/chaos/analogue-gravity/channel-framing works in the set, the operator-size phase-coherence diagnostic lens is absent and thus looks “new” there; however, that does not outweigh the explicit prior-art overlap in the immediate mechanism-diagnostics subliterature.

docs.title: Empirical Synthesis / Meta-Regularity — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Within the SYK/teleportation literature in this set, it is already recognized that (i) teleportation-like figures of merit can arise via multiple mechanisms (size-winding vs peaked-size/thermalization) and thus are not, by themselves, a certificate of holographic wormhole dynamics, and (ii) in specific SYK-like settings one can observe size-winding diagnostics and μ-sign-dependent asymmetries (at least within a model/ensemble). A particularly direct prior synthesis (Commuting SYK) already articulates the need to disambiguate mechanisms using size/phase diagnostics rather than teleportation performance alone.

What is Introduced: The statement packages these ingredients into a concrete, sufficient, multi-part operational discriminator intended to be applied across implementations: existence of a time/coupling window where arg q(l) is approximately linear across the dominant support of P(l), the coherence ratio R(l)=|q(l)|/P(l) is near 1 over that support, and flipping the sign of μ reverses/cancels the winding and yields a strong sign-asymmetry/enhancement in teleportation metrics. It further asserts a negative diagnostic: teleportation signals observed without (1)–(2) should not be attributed to the size-winding mechanism.

What is Novel: Aggregating across papers, the main novelty is not the individual components (size-winding diagnostics; μ-sign asymmetry; multiple mechanisms for teleportation-like signals) but the explicit triad-as-a-rule and its elevation to a cross-study certification criterion. The closest relevant work (Commuting SYK) substantially supports the same practical conclusion and mechanism taxonomy, making the proposed criterion best viewed as a derivable-but-previously-unstated meta-regularity/operationalization rather than a clearly new empirical law established by the provided literature; relative to more distant reviews/theory/analogue-gravity papers, the criterion appears genuinely new simply because they do not address these size-resolved teleportation diagnostics.

Contents:

Assessed theory: theory-6

docs.title: Dimensions
Phenomenon / Effect — Genuinely New
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed wormhole-teleportation/scrambling literature, the size-winding vs peaked-size (thermal-correlator-controlled) distinction is already articulated as two regimes that can both yield teleportation-like signatures, and some experimental/simulation works note that generic noise/Trotterization suppresses absolute fidelity/MI. However, none of the assessed papers explicitly isolate phase-randomization between operator-size sectors as the key noise knob, nor do they compare winding-based vs peaked-size teleportation under matched, controlled dephasing.

What is Introduced: The statement introduces a specific, mechanism-discriminating empirical prediction for NISQ implementations: phase-randomizing noise between size sectors (dephasing/phase diffusion/control-phase errors, including Trotter-like phase diffusion) should disproportionately suppress (i) sign-of-μ asymmetry and (ii) MI/fidelity peaks when teleportation relies on coherent size-winding (R(l)≈1 with linear arg q(l)), compared to regimes where teleportation is dominated by peaked-size/thermalization mechanisms without such coherence.

What is Novel: In the aggregated evidence, the closest papers establish the two mechanisms and report noise sensitivity in a general sense, but they do not formulate or demonstrate the differential fragility claim as an operational diagnostic (e.g., injected dephasing that selectively kills the winding-mediated signal while leaving peaked-size teleportation comparatively intact). Thus, relative to this set of papers, the mechanism-dependent dephasing fragility is not established and remains a novel, testable effect-level prediction.

docs.title: Explanatory / Mechanistic — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the most directly relevant SYK/teleportation analyses, traversable-wormhole-style teleportation is already explained as an interference effect that depends on organized operator-size phases (“size winding”) and quantified with size-resolved complex amplitudes (e.g., q(l)/Q_n) and coherence ratios (R(l)/r_n), while alternative teleportation-like signatures can arise from peaked-size/thermalization mechanisms without requiring cross-size phase alignment. These works generally do not propagate explicit, experimentally realistic phase-randomizing noise channels (dephasing/phase diffusion/control or Trotter-like phase errors) through the size-resolved formalism to predict selective degradation of winding-based signals versus peaked-size signals.

What is Introduced: The statement makes an explicit causal/mechanistic prediction: because size-winding teleportation relies on phase coherence across size sectors, noise that randomizes relative phases between size sectors should disproportionately suppress the sign-of-μ asymmetry and mutual-information/fidelity peaks in the coherent-winding regime (diagnosed by near-linear arg q(l) and R(l)≈1), compared to regimes where teleportation is dominated by peaked-size/thermalization magnitudes. It operationalizes a mechanism-discriminating test via injected/controlled dephasing (or identifiable phase-diffusion-like errors) and contrasts the expected fragility between the two mechanisms.

What is Novel: The underlying intuition that dephasing destroys interference is not new; given the already-articulated role of phase alignment in size-winding, the differential fragility claim is largely a consequence that could be derived from those formalisms but is not typically stated as a named, mechanism-separating prediction. The novelty is therefore mainly in elevating this consequence into a clear, testable, mechanism-dependent noise diagnostic (selective loss of sign-of-μ asymmetry and fidelity peaks under size-sector phase scrambling), rather than proposing a fundamentally new teleportation mechanism.

docs.title: Unification — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: At least one assessed paper already explicitly and centrally distinguishes two microscopic mechanisms that can generate similar traversable-wormhole/teleportation signatures—(i) phase-coherent operator-size winding and (ii) noncoherent peaked-size/thermalization—and provides size-resolved diagnostics demonstrating both regimes. Other assessed works connect wormhole-teleportation protocols to broader scrambling/decoding language and (in reviews) also discuss the winding vs peak-size distinction, but typically without elevating noise response as the key cross-platform discriminator.

What is Introduced: The statement ties the mechanism taxonomy to a specific operational discriminator based on phase-randomizing noise: controlled dephasing/phase diffusion between size sectors should disproportionately erase sign-of-μ asymmetry and mutual-information/fidelity peaks when the signal relies on coherent size-winding (R(l)≈1 and linear arg q(l)), compared to peaked-size/thermalization-dominated teleportation.

What is Novel: The unification of mechanisms itself (winding vs peaked-size/thermalization) is not novel given explicit-established prior articulation. What appears novel in aggregate is the elevation of mechanism-dependent dephasing fragility (and associated suppression of sign-of-μ asymmetry) as a general, experimentally actionable diagnostic principle for distinguishing the two mechanisms across NISQ implementations; this is largely a synthesis/extension built on existing mechanism separation rather than a new taxonomy.

docs.title: Generalization / Scope Expansion — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the provided holography/SYK/teleportation and quantum-simulation papers, NISQ relevance is frequently discussed (finite-N effects, Trotterization, calibration noise, platform feasibility), but typically without a general, mechanism-discriminating prescription that uses tunable phase-randomizing noise to test for operator-size phase coherence or “size-winding.” Some sources (especially the review and NISQ-motivated SYK-teleportation simulations) contain enough ingredients that one could plausibly anticipate that dephasing/phase-diffusion harms interference-based signatures, but they do not elevate this to a standard diagnostic contrasting size-winding vs peaked-size/thermalization mechanisms.

What is Introduced: The statement introduces a cross-platform, operational scope expansion: deliberately vary or inject noise that randomizes relative phases between operator-size sectors (dephasing, coherent control phase errors, Trotter-induced phase diffusion) and predict a differential effect—disproportionately suppressing sign-of-μ asymmetry and MI/fidelity peaks when those signatures rely on phase-coherent size-winding (R(l)≈1 and linear arg q(l)) compared to regimes where teleportation-like signals are dominated by peaked-size/thermalization mechanisms without such coherence.

What is Novel: In the aggregated evidence, essentially none of the papers explicitly establish this as a general principle or widely recognized experimental diagnostic for mechanism identification in two-sided wormhole-teleportation implementations. The closest countervailing evidence is that it appears inferable from the combination of (i) qualitative NISQ noise/Trotter discussions and (ii) the general understanding that dephasing destroys phase-sensitive interference, making the claim largely derivable rather than wholly unprecedented; however, as a concrete, mechanism-contrastive, experimentally actionable prescription centered on size-sector phase coherence and sign-of-μ asymmetry, it is not stated as such in these works.

docs.title: Constraint / Limitation — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed SYK/teleportation-facing literature (and reviews), it is already explicitly recognized that teleportation-like signatures (including sign-of-μ asymmetry and mutual-information/fidelity peaks) are not, by themselves, a sufficient certificate of holographic/traversable-wormhole dynamics, because non-holographic dynamics (e.g., commuting/integrable models, peaked-size distributions, or simple thermalization, especially at finite N and with postselection) can mimic these signals. Separately, many papers in adjacent analog-gravity/scrambling-measurement contexts discuss generic coherence fragility under experimental imperfections, but not framed as an operator-size-sector-specific discriminator for wormhole-teleportation mechanisms.

What is Introduced: The statement adds a specific, experimentally actionable limitation/diagnostic: when the mechanism is phase-coherent size-winding (R(l)≈1 over dominant support and approximately linear arg q(l)), then phase-randomizing noise between size sectors (dephasing, coherent-control phase noise, and Trotter-like phase diffusion) should disproportionately suppress hallmark observables (loss of sign-of-μ asymmetry and reduction/flattening of mutual-information/teleportation-fidelity peaks) compared to regimes where teleportation is dominated by peaked-size/thermalization mechanisms. It thereby proposes controlled injection or systematic variation/characterization of dephasing as a mechanism-discriminating test, not merely the generic claim that “noise reduces performance.”

What is Novel: No assessed paper explicitly formulates or tests this mechanism-dependent, size-sector-phase-specific dephasing fragility as an operational constraint/diagnostic for interpreting NISQ wormhole-teleportation experiments. The closest in-scope antecedents make the non-uniqueness/insufficiency point explicit and contain size-based or interference-based formalisms from which such fragility can plausibly be inferred, but they do not elevate the selective dephasing prediction (and its asymmetric impact on sign-of-μ effects) to an explicit result; thus the aggregate evidence supports the claim as largely derivable in hindsight rather than established.

docs.title: Conceptual Reframing / Abstraction — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Within the operator-size/teleportation subliterature, the core abstraction separating “peaked-size” (magnitude-dominated) teleportation-like signals from “size-winding/phase-coherent” mechanisms is already explicit, including size-resolved complex diagnostics that track both magnitudes and phases. Some review-style treatments already discuss size-winding conceptually, though not always with a single prescriptive operational checklist or a noise-fragility discriminator as the main experimental lever.

What is Introduced: The statement elevates “mechanism-dependent fragility to phase-randomizing noise” into a primary operational diagnostic: if teleportation relies on phase-coherent size-winding (linear arg q(l) and high R(l)), then injected dephasing/phase diffusion should disproportionately suppress sign-of-μ asymmetry and MI/fidelity peaks compared to regimes where teleportation arises from peaked-size/thermalization. It also packages this into an experimentally actionable probe (vary/characterize dephasing-like noise and compare responses across mechanisms).

What is Novel: Against papers that already build the size-basis magnitude/phase framework and explicitly distinguish peaked-size vs size-winding, the added content is mainly an operational emphasis (using dephasing fragility as a discriminant) rather than a new conceptual basis; this looks like a natural consequence of treating winding as an interference resource. Relative to the broader gravity/QI and simulation papers that do not use operator-size phase-coherence as a central lens, the reframing is new, but the strongest prior-art constraint in this set comes from work where the size-winding vs peaked-size distinction is already established.

docs.title: Empirical Synthesis / Meta-Regularity — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed literature, wormhole-inspired teleportation/scrambling diagnostics (e.g., mutual information/fidelity signatures, OTOC-based probes) are discussed and sometimes demonstrated on small-N simulations and hardware, and some works connect teleportation phenomenology to scrambling/size-distribution behavior. However, these papers generally do not articulate or document a cross-study regularity that mechanism-dependent teleportation signatures (phase-coherent size-winding vs peaked-size/thermalization) exhibit differential fragility specifically to phase-randomizing noise (dephasing/phase diffusion/control-phase errors), nor do they present controlled cross-mechanism noise-injection comparisons establishing such a pattern as “known.”

What is Introduced: The statement introduces a testable meta-regularity/diagnostic: teleportation signatures that depend on phase-coherent size-winding should be disproportionately suppressed by noise that randomizes relative phases between operator-size sectors, with an operational marker being the preferential loss of sign-of-μ asymmetry and MI/fidelity peaks under injected dephasing/phase diffusion. It further proposes that varying/engineering dephasing (or depth-induced phase diffusion) can discriminate winding-mediated (holographic/SYK-like) behavior from peaked-size/thermalization-driven teleportation that does not rely on such coherence.

What is Novel: Relative to the assessed papers, the specific cross-mechanism, cross-implementation noise-response rule (winding-based signatures being selectively more fragile to phase-randomizing noise than peaked-size/thermalization signatures, with suppression of sign-of-μ asymmetry as a key readout) is not presented as an established empirical synthesis and is not directly supported by an explicit multi-mechanism, controlled dephasing comparison. The strongest “least-novel” evidence is that the general intuition (coherent-interference effects are dephasing-sensitive) makes the claim plausibly derivable from background principles and review-level expectations, but it still appears unstated as a recognized meta-regularity linking operator-size phase coherence to diagnostic noise fragility of wormhole-teleportation signals.

docs.title: Novelty: Observable-first criterion for black-hole simulation
docs.text:
Contents:

  • Dimensions

Assessed theory: theory-1

docs.title: Dimensions
Phenomenon / Effect — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across analogue-gravity and holographic/QI toy-model literatures, papers already operationalize “black-hole(-like)” behavior by measuring specific signatures (thermal Hawking/Unruh spectra and correlations, OTOCs/chaos diagnostics, teleportation-through-wormhole correlators, Page-like transitions) under an explicit platform-to-model mapping and within some validity regime. At least some papers explicitly emphasize that a single signature is not a reliable, universal diagnostic (e.g., teleportation-like signals can occur without other holographic/chaotic indicators), motivating multi-observable validation.

What is Introduced: The statement elevates this into a general meta-level empirical/operational regularity: a black-hole simulation claim is well-posed only relative to an explicitly specified quadruple (O target observables, M mapping to device degrees of freedom, R validation relation(s) among observables, W validity/universality regime). It adds the explicit underdetermination claim: absent (O,M,R,W), different simulators can match one signature while disagreeing on others, so “we simulated a black hole” has insufficient content.

What is Novel: The underlying ingredients (choosing observables, providing a mapping, checking some relations, and discussing regime-of-validity) are largely already present as practice in many papers, and the caution about single-signature insufficiency is explicit in at least some. What appears novel in aggregate is the explicit formalization into a portable, prescriptive criterion/checklist (O,M,R,W) and the framing of “black-hole simulation” as an operational equivalence-class claim rather than a single phenomenon; this looks more like a synthesized principle than an established, named standard in the sampled literature.

docs.title: Explanatory / Mechanistic — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across analogue-gravity and holographic/quantum-information simulation papers, it is already standard (often implicit) to provide a concrete model-to-device mapping and to validate at least one targeted signature via a quantitative relation (e.g., Hawking/Unruh detailed-balance thermality; OTOC-based scrambling diagnostics; teleportation/decoding fidelity bounds). Several works also discuss, in domain-specific contexts, additional resource requirements for stronger information-theoretic claims (e.g., needing U and U*, postselection/amplification) and note ensemble/typicality caveats when comparing gravity path-integral results to single-instance Hamiltonians.

What is Introduced: The statement introduces an explicit, general operational prescription for when a “black-hole simulation” claim is well-posed: specify (O) a target observable set, (M) an explicit mapping making M(O) measurable, (R) at least one inter-observable validation relation to be preserved, and (W) a validity/universality regime. It also elevates scattered operational considerations into a unified explanatory rule that different experiments can be legitimately inequivalent (matching one signature but not others) and that stronger claims demand additional capabilities and clarified ensemble-vs-instance assumptions.

What is Novel: The aggregated evidence suggests the underlying physical mechanisms for particular signatures are not new (and in some cases are explicitly established), while the novelty lies in packaging existing practice into a compact, device-agnostic criterion (O,M,R,W) for claim well-posedness plus an explicit capability/assumption checklist for claim strength. Most surveyed papers either exemplify parts of (O,M,R,W) for a specific platform/model or discuss resources/ensemble issues piecemeal, but do not state this as a general necessary-condition rule; thus the statement is best viewed as a synthesizing mechanistic/operational abstraction rather than a new physical mechanism.

docs.title: Unification — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed papers, strong unification already exists within specific paradigms: analogue/QFT-in-curved-spacetime works provide explicit device mappings for horizon/QFT phenomena, and holography/quantum-information works unify scrambling, OTOCs, teleportation, and decoding diagnostics. Reviews/white papers and surveys often juxtapose analogue-gravity experiments with SYK/JT/teleportation/decoding programs and note they probe different signatures, but they typically do not formalize a field-level criterion that makes a “black-hole simulation” claim well-posed in an operationally comparable way.

What is Introduced: The statement introduces an explicit, general unifying taxonomy: a black-hole-simulation claim is only well-posed relative to an operational specification (O,M,R,W), and different experiments should be understood as belonging to potentially inequivalent operational equivalence classes defined by those choices. It also explicitly highlights a coarse but practical bifurcation (kinematic fixed-background QFT analogues vs holographic/quantum-information analogues) to explain why disparate demonstrations can be simultaneously legitimate yet not mutually validating the same “black-hole physics.”

What is Novel: The aggregated evidence indicates that the explicit (O,M,R,W) equivalence-class framing and the normative, cross-paradigm classification principle are generally not stated as such in the assessed literature; rather, they are at best inferable by synthesizing across disparate reviews, surveys, and platform-specific papers. One NISQ traversable-wormhole/SYK paper comes closest by integrating multiple diagnostics and validation checks into an operational workflow, but it still stops short of articulating the broader equivalence-class principle as a general organizing framework for all black-hole simulation claims.

docs.title: Generalization / Scope Expansion — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across analogue-gravity/QFT-in-curved-spacetime simulations and holographic/QI toy-model simulations, papers typically define a platform-specific mapping from some target model to device degrees of freedom and then validate one or a few signatures (e.g., Hawking/Unruh spectra, OTOCs/chaos, teleportation/decoding metrics), often with an implicit regime-of-validity. Reviews and community overviews already juxtapose many modalities and signatures, but they generally do not state a single, modality-independent criterion that must be satisfied for the claim “we simulated a black hole” to be well-posed.

What is Introduced: The statement introduces an explicit, modality-agnostic operational scoping requirement for black-hole-simulation claims: specify (O) the target observable set, (M) the mapping to measurable device quantities, (R) at least one validation relation among observables expected to be preserved, and (W) the regime/universality window where R should hold. It further asserts this applies uniformly across both major classes of “black-hole simulation” (kinematic analogue QFT mappings and holographic/quantum-information analogues) and elevates ensemble-vs-single-instance/typicality assumptions as part of what must be specified when comparing to gravity calculations.

What is Novel: Aggregated evidence suggests many ingredients are commonplace at the case-study level (papers already have some M and some checked observables), but the explicit elevation to a single prescriptive cross-modal standard (O,M,R,W) for what counts as a well-posed simulation claim is usually not stated as such. Some assessed papers support treating this as a synthesis/abstraction that follows naturally from comparing disparate signatures across subfields (i.e., “derivable but unstated”), while several others—especially narrow single-platform demonstrations or purely theoretical gravity papers—contain no comparable platform-spanning operational prescription, making the explicit cross-modal criterion appear genuinely new relative to those works. Overall, the best aggregate characterization is that the statement is a novel scope-expanding operational generalization: largely derivable from the literature in hindsight, but not established as an explicit community-wide criterion in the sampled papers.

docs.title: Constraint / Limitation — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across analogue-gravity and holography/quantum-information “black-hole simulation” literatures, papers routinely state platform-specific limitations (e.g., coordinate/boundary artifacts, finite-size/discretization, finite-N deviations, noise, resource demands like TFD preparation and U/U* access) and often caution that reproducing one signature (e.g., thermality or scrambling) is not sufficient to establish stronger claims. Several works also explicitly discuss averaging/typicality issues in technical form (e.g., Haar-averaging requirements; ensemble/replica-wormhole interpretations; code-subspace/state-dependence constraints), but typically inside their own problem setting rather than as a general criterion for simulator claims.

What is Introduced: The statement turns these scattered caveats into a prescriptive necessary-condition constraint on simulation claims: a “black-hole physics” simulation is well-posed only if it specifies (O) a target observable set, (M) an explicit mapping making M(O) measurable on the device, (R) at least one validation relation among observables in O that should be preserved under M, and (W) the regime where R is expected to hold. It further asserts that without (O,M,R,W) the claim is logically underdetermined because different simulators can match a single signature while disagreeing on others, and it elevates ensemble-vs-single-instance comparability (and associated typicality/code-subspace assumptions) to an explicit requirement when gravitational theory outputs are ensemble-averaged.

What is Novel: The aggregated evidence suggests the underlying limitations motivating caution are largely not new individually (many are explicit and, in reviews/white papers, fairly established), but the explicit “(O,M,R,W) checklist or the claim is underdetermined” principle is generally not stated as a named, cross-platform necessary-condition criterion in the surveyed papers. In some papers the ingredients appear in partial or peripheral form (e.g., noting insufficiency of single diagnostics; mentioning averaging/factorization caveats), so the novelty is best characterized as an abstraction/synthesis that makes implicit methodological requirements explicit and operational, rather than a newly discovered failure regime. Overall, this is strongest as a formalization that is mostly derivable from prior cautions, with pockets where it would read as genuinely new to narrower experimental papers that lack such meta-level criteria.

docs.title: Conceptual Reframing / Abstraction — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across analogue-gravity and holographic/quantum-information simulation papers, it is already common practice to (i) pick specific target diagnostics/observables, (ii) provide an explicit model-to-device mapping (e.g., discretization, effective-metric mapping, Jordan–Wigner), and (iii) validate by checking one or more expected relations or bounds within an assumed regime. At least one paper suggests this observable-oriented stance exists in the community as an (informal) methodology, but not as a named, prescriptive criterion for when a “black-hole simulation” claim is well-posed.

What is Introduced: The statement elevates this scattered practice into an explicit, normative meta-criterion: a claim of “simulating black-hole physics” is well-posed only relative to an operational specification (O, M, R, W), where R includes at least one relation among observables expected to be preserved under the mapping within a validity window. It thereby reframes simulation claims as membership in an operational equivalence class and asserts underdetermination when only a single signature is matched.

What is Novel: Aggregated evidence indicates the novelty is primarily the explicit abstraction/checklist (O,M,R,W) as the unit for stating, comparing, and adjudicating simulation claims across otherwise incommensurate platforms, rather than any new physical effect or diagnostic. However, multiple papers contain enough ingredients that this criterion is plausibly reconstructible as a synthesis (derivable-but-unstated), and one paper indicates components may be explicitly present but peripheral in experimental-holography practice; thus the contribution is best characterized as a novel formalization/standardization of an implicit norm, not a wholly unprecedented idea.

docs.title: Empirical Synthesis / Meta-Regularity — Derivable Unstated
docs.text:
What is Known: Across the assessed corpus—especially reviews/white papers—there is already a broad, explicit juxtaposition of multiple “black-hole-like” targets (Hawking/Unruh thermality, scrambling/OTOCs and level statistics, teleportation/wormhole and Hayden–Preskill-style decoding diagnostics, Page-curve/island ideas), and some sources explicitly discuss ensemble-averaged gravity calculations versus single-instance Hamiltonian realizations. However, these discussions are typically not presented as a single field-level rule for when a “black-hole simulation” claim is well-posed, nor as a standardized operational checklist that must accompany such claims.

What is Introduced: The statement elevates a cross-literature meta-regularity into an explicit criterion: a “black-hole simulation” claim is underdetermined unless it specifies an observable set O, a device mapping M making M(O) measurable, at least one validation relation R among observables expected to be preserved, and a regime W where that preservation is intended. It also systematizes the idea that multiple inequivalent simulator classes can each legitimately claim “black-hole simulation” (e.g., kinematic fixed-background QFT analogues vs holographic/quantum-information analogues), and makes ensemble-vs-single-instance comparability (typicality/averaging and code-subspace restrictions) part of the required specification rather than an optional interpretive caveat.

What is Novel: Relative to the assessed papers, the novelty lies primarily in codifying a prescriptive, observable-first comparison protocol (O,M,R,W) plus an explicit “single-signature is insufficient” underdetermination claim as a synthesized conclusion meant to apply across platforms and model families. The least-novel evidence comes from high-level syntheses (notably the Snowmass white paper) that already discuss many constituent ingredients (multiple targets; interpretational issues including ensemble vs single-instance), making the contribution best characterized as a stronger, centralized formulation and partially new synthesis rather than a wholly unprecedented discovery. Overall, the corpus supports that the statement is largely inferable from prior discussions but not commonly stated as an explicit, standard criterion.

Related Artifacts:

  • Operational Equivalence Classes for Quantum Black-Hole Simulation (revised)
